# Verdict: KILL. Do not launch control mechanics300 on the unchanged source

Launching it is not a useful bounded falsifier, because the result is already known. The CPUv3 run's own measured lifecycle shows that this source cannot finish the mechanics phase within 300 s, even with an infinitely fast GPU and zero extra mechanics work. Under the kill-on-failure rule, a predictable timeout would close the control arm and add one more permanent FAIL, without testing anything about correctness. Nothing I found points to a correctness defect in CPUv3. The blocker is the deadline the lifecycle has to fit into.

## What was actually measured

All of this comes from CPUv3 (`receipt.json`, `original.log`, `verification.json`) at invocation `a8bd65d9…`:

| Item | Seconds |
|---|---|
| Service time | 430.965 |
| Python wall time | 428.808 |
| Authority (admission) | 101.541 |
| Complete arm work | 239.505 |
| Arm work inside the candidate qualification | 231.457 |
| Exit tail (arm end at 341.8 s → receipt at 428.8 s), including measured rehash phases 22.9 + 12.8 + 0.75 + 6.56 | ≈87 |
| Single update core (CPU, includes its audit hashing) | 62.944 |

- **Event order:** the arm starts at about 102.3 s, the first reload ends at 107.8 s, and the two reloads in the public bundle check run at 336–341.8 s. That means the two public loads plus their mutant inference took only about 5.6 s, so serving inference is not where the time goes.
- **Host cost:** `/usr/bin/time` reports 141 % CPU and 318 M filesystem input blocks (about 163 GB re-read in 431 s). The lifecycle is bound by host hashing and disk I/O, not by the compute device.
- **Hash cache:** the fingerprint function has no cache by design ("No stat, version, or tensor-hash cache: every call reads current bytes"). On CUDA it also adds a device-side concatenate and a device-to-host copy, so moving to the GPU can only make hashing slower.

## Lower bound for mechanics300, using only measured CPUv3 numbers

Mechanics runs the same authority step (plus admitting the `selected_cpu` receipt) and the same arm steps: fresh construction, the mutant checks, two image checks, save, restore, export and two public loads. Its exit is heavier, because `audit_origin_diagnostics` only runs when the phase is not CPU. Its only real saving is device compute. Even so:

430.97 − 62.94 (the whole CPU update, generously treated as device work) − 8.05 (the second-seed initializer check, which only the CPU phase does) − 20 (a generous allowance for CPU witness inference) ≈ **340 s, which is already over 300 s.**

The mechanics path then adds work on top of that. The per-call costs below come from `connected-mlp-cpu-phase-diag-v2`, which ran on older source:

| Extra mechanics work | Seconds |
|---|---|
| One more fresh construction | ~34.8 |
| One more restore | ~22.5 |
| Two more saves | ~8–12 |
| 33 more updates, host audit cost only | ~185 |

The per-update audit cost follows from the frozen `update()`. It calls `integrity()` at the start and the end (about 1.91 s each), plus `encoder_facts` (1.16 s), plus the payload fingerprint. Each of these re-hashes the 1.7 GB encoder, so the total is about 9 full-encoder hashes and about 5.6 s per update before any GPU work. The control arm pays the same cost.

My estimate for the GPU mechanics run is **about 650–750 s.** That figure is an estimate: the CUDA cost of each integrity call has never been measured. The **≥340 s lower bound does not depend on that**, because it uses only CPUv3 measurements.

The earlier mechanics passes (231–256 s) all come from the cached-feature line with a frozen encoder. They are not evidence that this connected-encoder source can fit in 300 s. The old Opus feasibility concern was an estimate, and the full CPU result now confirms it with measurements.

## The same problem hits TRAIN600 and the cost ratio

- **TRAIN600:** 128 updates × about 5.6 s of host audit alone is about 717 s, before the roughly 190 s of fixed lifecycle and any GPU time. So 600 s cannot be met either. Fixing only the mechanics deadline would just move the timeout to TRAIN.
- **The ≤1.50 core-time gate:** both arms re-hash the same 1.7 GB encoder several times per update, so the "core" time is dominated by audit work that is identical in both arms. The ratio will sit near 1.0 by construction. A pass would tell you almost nothing about the method's speed, which is the speed half of the production goal.

## Smallest correction before any launch

This does not involve hash skips, state caches, a new loss, or a blanket cap.

1. **Measure first, without qualifying anything.** Run one CUDA phase observation of the exact frozen mechanics path, in the same style as `connected-mlp-cpu-phase-diag-v2`: no qualification, no state reuse, results labelled as diagnostic. It should record CUDA timings for `integrity`, `encoder_facts`, `fingerprint`, `fresh`, `restore`, `save`, and the update core. That per-call CUDA cost is the one missing piece of evidence. The observation will also time out, but by design and without consuming the arm.
2. **Then make one decision before launching anything, and get it reviewed.** There are two options:
   - **(a) Re-derive the mechanics and TRAIN budgets** from the measured cost model: CPUv3's fixed lifecycle, plus the measured CUDA per-call cost times the exact call counts from the frozen source, plus a stated margin. This changes the `policy()` at line 122, the launch `resource_policy` and `RuntimeMaxSec`. A budget derived this way is not a blanket cap, because the 300/600 constants were inherited from the cached-feature line and are now shown to be wrong for this source.
   - **(b) If budgets must not change at all,** the connected-MLP method cannot be qualified on this source line. Removing duplicate back-to-back `integrity()` calls inside `update()` would save at most about 65 s, which is well short of the ≥40 s already over the limit plus the 33 extra updates. In that case the honest call is KILL for the whole family, not a retry.

Until option 1 is done and one of 2a or 2b is chosen, launch neither the control nor the candidate mechanics. All earlier timeouts remain FAIL.

## Limitations of this review

- The per-call audit costs come from v2 source. v3 batched the witness reads (authority dropped from 135.8 s to 101.5 s), so per-call costs in v3 may be lower. The ≥340 s lower bound does not rely on them.
- The 62.9 s CPU update mixes forward-pass and hashing time with no split inside it.
- The one GPU number that would close the question, the CUDA cost of each integrity call, does not exist yet.
